source_text: 1. Cvum enim ex Seripturis arguuntur, in accusationem con-vertuntur ipsarum Seripturarum, quasi non recte habeant, neque sint ex auctoritate, et quia varie sint dictez, et quia non possit ex his inveniri veritas ab his qui nesciant traditionem. Non enim per literas traditam illam, sed per vivam vocem: ob quam causam et Paulum dixisse: Sapientiam autem loquimur inter perfectos: sapientiam autem non mundi hujus. Et hane sapientiam unusquisque eorum esse dicit, quam a semetipso adinvenit, fictionem videlicet, ut digne secundum eos sit veritas, aliquando quidem in Valentino, aliquando autem in Marcione, aliquando in Cerintho, postea deinde in Basilide, fuit aut et in illo qui contra disputat, qui nihil salutare loqui potuit. Unusquisque enim ipsorum omnimodo perversus, semetipsum regulam veritatis depravans preedicare non confunditur, ' 2. Cum autem ad eam iterum traditionem, que est ab Apostolis, quee per successiones Presbyterorum in Ecclesiis. custoditur, provocamus eos, adversantur traditioni, dicentes se non solum Presbyteris, sed etiam A postolis exsistentes sapientiores, sinceram invenisse veritatem. Apostolos enim admiscuisse ea que sunt legalia Salvatoris verbis: et non solum Apostolos, sed etiam ipsum Dominum, modo quidem a Demiurgo, modo autem a medietate, interdum autem a summitate fecisse sermones : se vero indubitate, et intaminate, et sincere absconditum scire mysterium: quod quidem impudentissime est blasphemare suum factorem. Eyenit itaque, neque Scripturis jam, neque traditioni consentire eos. Adversus tales certamen nobis est, o dilectissime, more serpentum lubrici [7. lubrice] undique effugere conantes. Quapropter undique resistendum est illis, si quos ex his retusione confundentes, ad conversionem veritatis adducere possimus. Etenim si non facile est ab errore apprehensam resipiscere animam, sed non omnimodo impossibile est errorem effugere apposita veritate.
pass_a_gloss: For when they are argued against from the Scriptures, they turn into an accusation of the Scriptures themselves, as if they do not have them rightly, nor are they from authority, and because they have been said in various ways, and because truth cannot be found from these things by those who do not know the tradition. For it has not been handed down through letters, but through living voice, on account of which reason also Paul said: We speak wisdom among the perfect, wisdom however not of this world. And each one of them says that this wisdom is what he himself has discovered, evidently a fiction, so that truth may be worthy according to them, sometimes indeed in Valentinus, sometimes however in Marcion, sometimes in Cerinthus, afterwards then in Basilides, and also in that one who disputes against, who was not able to speak anything saving. For each one of them, being entirely perverted, preaches without being confounded, depraving himself as a rule of truth. When however we provoke them to that tradition which is from the Apostles, which is kept through the successions of Presbyters in the Churches, they oppose the tradition, saying that they have found the pure truth, not only more wise than the Presbyters, but also than the Apostles themselves. For they say that the Apostles have mixed those things which are legal with the words of the Savior, and not only the Apostles, but also the Lord Himself, sometimes from the Demiurge, sometimes however from the middle, sometimes however from the top, have made speeches, but they themselves undoubtedly, and undefiled, and purely know the hidden mystery, which indeed is to blaspheme their maker most impudently. They do not agree therefore with either the Scriptures or the tradition. The struggle against such people is ours, O most beloved, as serpents slippery in every way, trying to escape. Wherefore it must be resisted on all sides, if we can confound some of them by refutation, and lead them to the conversion of truth. For if it is not easy for a soul seized by error to recover, it is not entirely impossible to escape error, with truth applied.

bible_refs.note: We speak wisdom among the perfect

pass_b_english:
When they are confronted with Scripture, they turn their attack against Scripture itself, claiming it is not rightly preserved, lacks authority, contradicts itself in its varied expressions, and cannot yield truth to those who lack the tradition. For that tradition was not handed down in writing but by living voice — which is why Paul declared, "We speak wisdom among the perfect, but not the wisdom of this world" (1 Corinthians 2:6). Each of these teachers claims that this wisdom is his own private discovery, a mere invention, so that truth might be whatever suits him: one moment it appears in Valentinus, another in Marcion, then in Cerinthus, later in Basilides, even in the one who argues against the rest yet could speak nothing that saves. Every single one of them is thoroughly perverted; without shame each makes himself the rule of truth, distorting it as he preaches.

But when we appeal to the tradition that comes from the Apostles — the tradition guarded through the succession of presbyters in the churches — they reject it, boasting that they have found the pure truth and are wiser not only than the presbyters but than the Apostles themselves. They allege that the Apostles mixed legal ordinances with the Savior's words, and that even the Lord Himself spoke sometimes from the Demiurge, sometimes from the middle realm, sometimes from the highest summit. Meanwhile they claim to know the hidden mystery without doubt, without stain, purely — which is nothing less than the most brazen blasphemy against their own Maker. Consequently they agree with neither Scripture nor tradition. Our struggle, dear friend, is against such men, who like slippery serpents try to wriggle free on every side. Therefore they must be resisted on every front, so that by refuting them we may confound some and lead them to the conversion of truth. For though it is not easy for a soul seized by error to recover, it is not utterly impossible to escape error when truth is applied.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent English version that maintains the theological nuances and agency of the original. The scripture citation (1 Corinthians 2:6) correctly identifies the allusion in 'Sapientiam autem loquimur inter perfectos'.
